The House was asked to suspend standing orders to allow the immediate introduction and debate of the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment Bill 2014 [No. 3], the Road Safety Remuneration Repeal Bill 2016, and the Road Safety Remuneration Amendment (Protecting Owner Drivers) Bill 2016. The speaker argued the Fair Work bill, passed three times by the House, targets dishonest union leaders, while the Road Safety bills address the impact on owner drivers from Labor’s previous legislation.

The speaker argued against repealing the Road Safety Remuneration Tribunal, citing 25 heavy-vehicle-related road deaths last month and over 300 last year, and presenting evidence from PwC, NTC, and academic reports that link pay rates to safety. He named truck driver John Waltis, who had attended 52 funerals of killed drivers, and quoted Senator John Williams and researchers Michael Quinlan and Michael Belzer in support of the tribunal's role in preventing unsafe practices.

The speaker argued that the Road Safety Remuneration Tribunal should be repealed because it discriminates against owner-driver truck drivers by imposing above-market rates that only apply to them, not to large companies or employed drivers, causing owner-operators to lose contracts and park their trucks. The speaker cited examples of a driver named Greg from Melbourne and a contractor from Tomingley who could no longer compete, and noted that the coalition opposed the tribunal when it was established in 2012.

The speaker opposed the Road Safety Remuneration Amendment Bill, arguing that the 2016 order imposes unfair price fixing and fines of up to $54,000 on owner-drivers while ignoring real safety issues, and called for the tribunal to be abolished.

The speaker argued that the Road Safety Remuneration Tribunal is a Labor-union initiative that unfairly targets owner-operator truck drivers, and supported the repeal bill to prevent a ruling that would impose minimum rates and cost the economy $2.3 billion over 15 years while threatening 3,500 jobs. He named several owner-operators from South Australia who would be driven out of business, and criticised the shadow minister for linking the tribunal's ruling to a fatal accident without evidence.

Moved to suspend standing order 133 (deferred divisions on Mondays and Tuesdays) until the conclusion of consideration of the Road Safety Remuneration Repeal Bill 2016 and the Road Safety Remuneration Amendment (Protecting Owner Drivers) Bill 2016, to allow a vote on the RSRT at the earliest convenience of the House.

The speaker supported the Road Safety Remuneration Amendment Bill 2016 to delay the contractor-driver minimum payment order to 1 January 2017, arguing that the industry—employing 200,000 drivers with 35,000 owner-drivers at risk—needed time to adjust due to widespread misunderstanding of the order and potential business viability issues.

The speaker argued that the Road Safety Remuneration Tribunal order was designed to make owner-drivers uncompetitive and destroy small businesses, citing a $54,000 fine threat to contractor Bryan Alley, and announced the Road Safety Remuneration Amendment (Protecting Owner Drivers) Bill 2016 as a backup to defer the order until 2017 if the Senate rejects the repeal bill.

Labor opposed the Road Safety Remuneration Amendment (Protecting Owner Drivers) Bill 2016, arguing the government should delay the tribunal’s December order and consult affected parties rather than abolish the tribunal, which it called disproportionate. The speech emphasised improving road safety without harming owner-drivers and highlighted industry-wide problems with large companies paying drivers late.

The majority voted to speed up the passage of the bills so that they could immediately vote on whether to pass it. In parliamentary jargon, they voted to suspend the [standing and sessional orders](http://www.peo.gov.au/learning/fact-sheets/standing-orders.html) that would have stopped the bills from being passed immediately (ordinarily, they couldn't be passed until the next sitting day). ### What were the bills about? The bills re-institute a workplace relations framework that was first put in place back in 2005. Among other things, they re-establish the [Australian Building and Construction Commissioner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Office_of_the_Australian_Building_and_Construction_Commissioner) and re-introduce provisions dealing with unlawful [industrial action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Industrial_action) and coercion that are specific to the building industry. Read more in the [bills digest](http://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd1314a/14bd034).

Building and Construction Industry (Improving Productivity) Bill 2013 [No. 2] and one other - Second Reading - Agree with the bills' main idea
The speaker presented the Building and Construction Industry (Improving Productivity) Bill 2013 [No. 2] and its explanatory memorandum, expressing gratitude to the Manager of Opposition Business.

The government reintroduced the Building and Construction Industry (Improving Productivity) Bill 2013 [No. 2] to re-establish the Australian Building and Construction Commission, arguing the construction sector—which directly employs over a million Australians—needs regulation to prevent intimidation and job-destroying conflict. The speech cited the Heydon royal commission as incontrovertible evidence of a massive cultural problem in the industry.

The speaker opposed the bill to re-establish the Australian Building and Construction Commission, arguing it unfairly targets construction workers and that the government's $80 million royal commission produced no criminal convictions. They announced Labor's alternative reforms to protect workers' rights, including increased penalties for underpayment and sham contracting.

The speaker argued for re-establishing the Australian Building and Construction Commission (ABCC) to address lawlessness and corruption in the construction industry, citing the Royal Commission into Trade Union Governance and Corruption and noting that CFMEU-related unions and officials have been fined over $6 million since 2005. The speaker also stated that the ABCC previously led to 9% productivity growth and $7.5 billion in annual consumer savings, and criticised Labor and the Greens for opposing the bill despite a perceived electoral mandate.

The speaker opposed the Building and Construction Industry (Improving Productivity) Bill 2013 [No. 2] to re-establish the Australian Building and Construction Commission, arguing its coercive powers are excessive and undemocratic, and announced Labor’s alternative plan to increase penalties for employer exploitation, strengthen protections against sham contracting, and give the Fair Work Ombudsman more powers.

The speaker argued for re-establishing the Australian Building and Construction Commission (ABCC) to reverse Labor's 2012 abolition, citing a 2013 election commitment and citing threats to contractors in the Macquarie electorate and CFMEU actions in Adelaide. The bill introduces a new building code, prevents contractors breaching safety or migration laws from Commonwealth-funded work, and imposes penalties for unlawful industrial action.

The Building and Construction Industry (Improving Productivity) Bill 2013 [No. 2] was argued to re-establish the Australian Building and Construction Commission, citing a 9% productivity increase and $7.5 billion annual savings during its previous operation, which was abolished by Labor in 2012.

The bill was opposed for granting the Australian Building and Construction Commission coercive powers without judicial oversight, removing protections against self-incrimination and natural justice. Labor’s alternative plan proposes increased penalties for employer exploitation, stronger Fair Work Ombudsman powers, and support for unions to reduce inequality.

The speaker argued for the Building and Construction Industry (Improving Productivity) Bill 2013 [No.2], claiming the Australian Building and Construction Commission saved $6.3 billion annually before its 2012 abolition, and accused Labor of being puppets of union bosses. He cited Dyson Heydon's royal commission finding of "widespread and deep-seated" corruption in unions and stated the bill would restore rule of law, reduce violence and productivity losses in the construction industry.

The speaker argued that the Building and Construction Industry (Improving Productivity) Bill 2013 [No. 2] is an ideological attack on construction workers and the CFMEU, claiming it would increase workplace injuries and deaths while ignoring exploitation of temporary visa workers. They opposed the bill, citing the CFMEU’s role in safety support and community activities, and called for its withdrawal.

The speaker opposed the Building and Construction Industry (Improving Productivity) Bill 2013 [No.2], arguing it re‑establishes the Australian Building and Construction Commission with oppressive, coercive powers that target construction workers, and called it the start of a return to Work Choices.

The speaker supported the original Building and Construction Industry (Improving Productivity) Bill 2013 [No. 2] and argued the Australian Building and Construction Commission (ABCC) is necessary to reduce lawlessness, intimidation, and lost productivity in the construction sector, citing 12,300 days lost to industrial action in Queensland in 2014 and a $40,000–$50,000 cost difference per unit between CFMEU and non-union construction. He also criticised the federal safety office’s accreditation costs ($200,000–$400,000 initial, $100,000–$200,000 annually) as a barrier for regional small-to-medium enterprises.

The speaker opposed the Building and Construction Industry (Improving Productivity) Bill 2013 [No. 2], arguing it removes the right to silence and limits union entry, threatening civil liberties and worker safety; they noted 25 construction deaths in 2015 and criticised the opposition for focusing on royal commission smears rather than the bill's substance, adding that the previous royal commission resulted in no criminal convictions.

The speaker argued for the Building and Construction Industry (Improving Productivity) Bill 2013 [No. 2], supporting the restoration of the Australian Building and Construction Commission to address lawlessness, intimidation and corruption in the construction sector, and cited a 9% productivity gain and $7.5 billion annual consumer benefit under the previous ABCC.

The speaker opposed the Building and Construction Industry (Improving Productivity) Bill 2013, arguing it provides unprecedented coercive powers, is based on discredited productivity evidence (Econtech modelling), and would increase workplace fatalities—citing 36 deaths in 2007-08, double the rate before the ABCC, and noting the Cole royal commission referred 31 individuals with no prosecutions.

The speaker argued that the Building and Construction Industry (Improving Productivity) Bill 2013 [No. 2] must be passed to re-establish the Australian Building and Construction Commission, citing productivity gains of $3.1 billion per year within two years of its original creation, rising to $6.3–7.5 billion annually, and noting 93 referrals for civil and criminal proceedings from the Heydon royal commission as evidence of ongoing corruption.

The speaker argued for re-establishing the Australian Building and Construction Commission (ABCC) to improve productivity and deter unlawful industrial action, citing the Stella Maris commission of inquiry where the Northern Territory Labor government improperly gifted a site to Unions NT, and Labor ministers Delia Lawrie and Gerry McCarthy were found to have acted unaccountably.

The speaker argued for the re-establishment of the Australian Building and Construction Commission (ABCC) via the Building and Construction Industry (Improving Productivity) Bill 2013, citing corruption, lawlessness and productivity losses in the construction industry. They highlighted the CFMEU’s black-ban on Boral costing over $20 million and a $4 million settlement, and claimed the previous ABCC brought nine per cent productivity growth and $7.5 billion in consumer savings.

The speaker opposed the Building and Construction Industry (Improving Productivity) Bill 2013 [No. 2], arguing it is based on ideology rather than evidence and represents an attack on workers' rights, while Labor's alternative agenda focuses on cracking down on illegal underpayment, sham contracts, and protecting temporary overseas workers.

The speaker opposed the Building and Construction Industry (Improving Productivity) Bill 2013 and its reintroduction of the ABCC, arguing it would undermine workers' safety and civil liberties by removing rights to silence, legal representation, and protection against self-incrimination. Labor proposed alternative reforms including $4.5 million for increased monitoring of registered organisations, higher penalties for underpayment, and stronger whistleblower protections.

The speaker supported the Building and Construction Industry (Improving Productivity) Bill 2013 [No. 2], criticised the opposition for opposing stronger workplace laws, and noted being forced into a union with no choice.

The speaker opposed the Building and Construction Industry (Improving Productivity) Bill 2013 [No.2], arguing it infringes human rights and is based on a false premise, and noted that the $60 million Cole royal commission produced no criminal prosecutions while 11,000 workers needed $22.3 million in back pay recovered by the Fair Work Ombudsman.

The speaker argued for re‑establishing the Australian Building and Construction Commission (ABCC) through the Building and Construction Industry (Improving Productivity) Bill 2013 [No. 2], contending that Labor’s 2012 abolition had led to increased industrial unlawfulness and that the new watchdog would improve productivity and protect workers and employers in the construction sector.
This bill would reintroduce three measures from the 2015 Budget that were removed from an earlier bill in June 2015.

It would cut from two weeks to six weeks the period that age pension and certain other payment recipients receive their full basic rate while overseas, then adjust payments based on Australian working life residence.

The bill would also freeze income free areas for working age allowances and student payments from 1 July 2016 and 1 January 2016 respectively, and cease the pensioner education supplement from 1 January 2016.
Reduces the portability period for age pension and some other payments from two weeks to six weeks.
Freezes income free areas for working age allowances and student payments for three years.
Ends the pensioner education supplement from 1 January 2016.
Age pension recipients and a small number of people on other payments with unlimited portability, as well as recipients of working age allowances and student payments.
Social Services Legislation Amendment (Budget Repair) Bill 2015 - Second Reading - Agree with the bill's main idea

The speaker argued that the Social Services Legislation Amendment (Budget Repair) Bill 2015 is necessary to address a $100 million daily interest bill on debt accrued under the previous Labor government, which left $191 billion in deficits and $123 billion in projected deficits. The speaker stated that the bill does not cut pensions for those who have lived in Australia for 35 years, but introduces a six-week overseas portability limit with proportional reductions for shorter residency, and saves $500 million by removing outdated education supplements.

The speaker argued the government unfairly targets low-income Australians, pensioners, and unemployed youth with budget cuts while protecting wealthy superannuants and multinationals avoiding tax. Specific measures criticised include changing overseas pension payments, abolishing the pensioner education supplement, and freezing income-free areas for working-age allowances, which the speaker said would push more people into poverty, citing 30% of Bendigo’s electorate surviving on under $600 per week.

The speaker argued that the Social Services Legislation Amendment (Budget Repair) Bill 2015 is essential for Australia's long-term economic health, citing Labor's $191 billion in deficits and a projected $667 billion deficit without policy change.

The speaker opposed the Social Services Legislation Amendment (Budget Repair) Bill 2015, arguing it unfairly targets vulnerable Australians, particularly pensioners, by cutting overseas pension payments after six weeks, abolishing the pensioner education supplement and education entry payment, and pausing indexation. They also criticised the government for doubling the deficit and for its record on pensioner cuts since 2013.

Opposition members opposed the Social Services Legislation Amendment (Budget Repair) Bill 2015, which included measures affecting pensioners travelling overseas, cuts to the pensioner education supplement and education entry payment, and changes to indexation.

The speaker argued that the budget is in desperate need of repair, citing nine consecutive years of deficits, daily borrowing of $100 million, and $14 billion in annual interest payments, and quoted former Labor Prime Minister Paul Keating in support of spending cuts.

The speaker opposed the Social Services Legislation Amendment (Budget Repair) Bill 2015, arguing it unfairly cuts the overseas pension payment period from 26 weeks to six weeks and abolishes the pensioner education supplement and education entry payment. Labor will not support the bill.

The speaker opposed the Social Services Legislation Amendment (Budget Repair) Bill 2015, arguing it targets older Australians and vulnerable people, and highlighted three measures: reducing overseas pension portability from 26 to 6 weeks, abolishing the pensioner education supplement affecting 41,300 people (mostly women), and abolishing the education entry payment affecting 87,000 people.

The speaker opposed the Social Services Legislation Amendment (Budget Repair) Bill 2015, arguing it would cut age pension payments for migrants who travel overseas for more than six weeks, creating a discriminatory system that saves $168.4 million over four years at the expense of vulnerable pensioners.

The speaker opposed the Social Services Legislation Amendment (Budget Repair) Bill 2015, arguing it unfairly targets vulnerable groups. The bill would reduce pension portability for overseas visits from 26 weeks to six weeks for those with fewer than 35 years of Australian work history, abolish the $208 education entry payment for 87,000 recipients, and cut the pensioner education supplement of $31–$61 per fortnight for 41,130 people, three-quarters of whom are women.

The MP opposed the Social Services Legislation Amendment (Budget Repair) Bill 2015, arguing it unfairly cuts $579 million from pensioners and students, including abolishing the pensioner education supplement and education entry payment, and restricting overseas pension portability to six weeks for those who have lived in Australia less than 35 years. The MP also cited broader government policies—such as pension asset-test changes, increased pension age, and possible GST rises—as disproportionately hitting low- and middle-income Australians.

The government argued that reducing the portability period for age pension payments overseas from 26 weeks to six weeks, saving $168 million, is necessary for budget repair and fairness, as Australia is one of few nations paying a non-contributory pension abroad indefinitely. The bill also reintroduces measures to cease the pensioner education supplement and education entry payment, and freeze indexation of income-free areas for three years.
Social Services Legislation Amendment (Family Payments Structural Reform and Participation Measures) Bill (No. 2) 2015 - Second Reading - Agree with bill's main idea

The speaker opposed the Social Services Legislation Amendment (Family Payments Structural Reform and Participation Measures) Bill (No. 2) 2015, arguing it would cut $16 billion from low- and middle-income families over ten years, including up to $5,000 annually for single-parent families, and called on the Liberal-National government to abandon the cuts.

The coalition argued the family payments bill is necessary to repair the budget, blaming Labor for a record deficit that now requires $13 billion a year in interest payments and a decade of projected deficits; the member also noted the nation borrows another $1.4 million every 20 minutes.

The bill increases family tax benefit A by $10 per fortnight for some families and introduces a $1,000 annual payment for families with children under one, but cuts family tax benefit B for single parents with children aged 13–16 (by around $1,700–$3,100), abolishes it for single parents whose youngest child is 17–19 and in secondary school, and phases out end-of-year supplements over two years. The speaker criticised the government for targeting vulnerable families instead of closing tax loopholes for multinational companies and wealthy superannuants.

The bill increases Family Tax Benefit Part A fortnightly rates by $10 per child aged up to 19, raises Family Tax Benefit Part B by $1,000 per year for families with a youngest child under one, and phases out FTB Part A and Part B supplements, aiming to achieve long-term sustainability of family payments while targeting support to vulnerable families.

The speaker argued that the government faces a fiscal crisis due to ongoing budget deficits, with expenditure still 10% higher than revenue, and blamed the Labor Party for creating the problem and blocking savings measures. He announced the Social Services Legislation Amendment Bill as a set of reasonable savings measures to restrain spending, including phasing out family tax benefit supplements and introducing a new rate structure for Family Tax Benefit Part B, while increasing Family Tax Benefit Part A payments by about $10 per child aged up to 19.

The speaker opposed the Social Services Legislation Amendment Bill, arguing it unfairly cuts family tax benefits A and B, affecting 1.3 million families losing the FTB B supplement and 1.5 million losing the FTB A supplement, with a single mother of two potentially $5,000 worse off annually. The speaker noted their electorate has an average household income of $53,000 and contains 52% of NSW families living with autism, mostly single-parent households.

The bill reforms family tax benefit rates and aligns youth allowance for under-18s living at home with family tax benefit rates from 1 July 2018 to remove financial incentives to leave school. The speaker supported the bill, noting that in the electorate of Murray, low income growth, high youth unemployment (26–27%), and water policy impacts have increased reliance on welfare.

The speaker opposed the Social Services Legislation Amendment (Family Payments Structural Reform and Participation Measures) Bill (No. 2) 2015, arguing it would cut Family Tax Benefit A and B for over 20,000 families in each of several regional electorates, including their own, and disproportionately harm working poor, single parents, and grandparent carers.

The speaker opposed the Social Services Legislation Amendment (Family Payments Structural Reform and Participation Measures) Bill (No. 2) 2015, arguing it unfairly targets low- and middle-income families and single parents, with specific cuts including 1.5 million families losing the family tax benefit part A supplement (over $700 per child per year) and 1.3 million losing the part B supplement (over $350 per family per year), while single parents with children over 13 would lose $1,700 annually and those with children over 16 would lose $3,100.

The speaker supported the bill to increase Family Tax Benefit Part A by $10 a fortnight, reform Part B with a $1,000 annual increase for families with a child under one, phase out end-of-year supplements, and reinvest savings into the $3 billion Jobs for Families childcare package.

The speaker argued that the government must live within its means and supported the Social Services Legislation Amendment (Family Payments Structural Reform and Participation Measures) Bill (No. 2) 2015, which includes increasing Family Tax Benefit Part A by about $10 per fortnight per child up to age 19, introducing a new rate structure for Part B, and phasing out Part A and Part B supplements. He criticised the opposition and crossbenchers for blocking budget repair measures, citing the need to address the $150 billion annual social security budget and encourage workforce participation.

The speaker opposed the Social Services Legislation Amendment (Family Payments Structural Reform and Participation Measures) Bill (No. 2) 2015, arguing it unfairly cuts family payments—leaving single parents up to $5,000 a year worse off—and criticised the government for $80 billion in health and education cuts and a proposed 15% GST. Specific figures cited include 1.5 million families losing FTB A supplements of over $700 per child annually, 136,000 single parents with children aged 13–16 facing a $1,700 cut, and Labor’s $37 billion investment in the Gonski education plan.

The speaker supported the Social Services Legislation Amendment Bill (No. 2) 2015, which phases out family tax benefit supplements, increases FTB Part A rates by $10 per child, and introduces a new FTB Part B rate structure, with savings partly funding the $3 billion Jobs for Families Child Care Package. The speaker also noted that $12 billion a year is spent on interest from Labor's debt.

The speaker supported the Social Services Legislation Amendment Bill, which increases Family Tax Benefit Part A by about $10 per fortnight per child for 1.2 million families, raises Part B by $1,000 per year for families with a child under one, and phases out end-of-year supplements to save over $4 billion. The speaker also promoted the Jobs for Families childcare package and criticised Labor’s record on family payments.

The speaker argued that the Turnbull government's policies remain as unfair as the Abbott government's, citing the Social Services Legislation Amendment Bill as cutting $16 billion from family payments over ten years. They claimed Labor supported $9 billion in reasonable cuts but opposed these harsh measures, noting the government doubled the deficit to $38 billion and should instead tackle tax avoidance and wealthy tax breaks.

The bill increases Family Tax Benefit Part A fortnightly payments by $10.08 per child for around 1.2 million lower-income families, aligns youth allowance rates, and phases out the Part A and B supplements by 2018, saving $4.1 billion. It also raises the maximum Family Tax Benefit Part B rate by $1,000.10 for families with a youngest child under 12 months and ends Part B for single parents when the youngest child turns 16, while exempting grandparent carers and single parents aged 60 and over, with the package funding the Jobs for Families childcare reforms.

Described a delegation to Myanmar observing GAVI vaccination work and argued that its partnership model delivers effective aid, strengthens health systems and saves lives.
